walkthroughs.body_html:
The Role of Markets and Money — a core area of GCSE Economics.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

The Role of Markets and Money brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with The Role of Markets and Money.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: A market with one seller is a:
options: Perfect competition
Monopoly
Oligopoly
Monopsony

mcqs.q: The price mechanism performs three functions; which is NOT one?
options: Signalling
Incentivising
Rationing
Producing

mcqs.q: What are the functions of money?
options: Medium of exchange, store of value, unit of account, and standard of deferred payment — money must perform these to function as money.
Money is only valuable if backed by gold.
Price ceilings only affect the rich.
Money is valuable because it is made of valuable materials.

mcqs.q: What is the predicted effect of a binding price ceiling like rent control?
options: Price ceilings make goods cheaper for everyone with no downsides.
Shortage in the market — quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied at the controlled price, leading to queues, black markets and reduced quality.
QE is when banks charge negative interest on deposits.
Price ceilings only affect the rich.

mcqs.q: How does quantitative easing actually work?
options: The central bank creates reserves to buy financial assets (mostly government bonds) from banks and pension funds, raising asset prices and lowering yields — stimulating spending and lending indirectly. It is not literally printing physical cash for the public.
QE is the central bank printing money and handing it to citizens.
Money is only valuable if backed by gold.
QE is when banks charge negative interest on deposits.
